doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

chapter: Mingus, road life and the jazz economy
title: Pearl Bailey on musicians pricing themselves out; club costs
summary: May recalls Pearl Bailey's views on musicians leaving to lead bands, and discusses club costs and just wanting to play.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: It is. It’s very expensive. If you don’t put a hundred bucks in your pocket, you might not have enough, to take your wife out, just to go to the club, not to have dinner and all that. So it’s pretty expensive. And I remember Pearl Bailey told — I used to fill in for Milt Hinton when Milt couldn’t make a gig or something like that I would go to Jordan’s say for instance with Pearl. She was so wonderful to be with. And she would say that it’s a shame that jazz musicians are kind of pricing themselves out of the business. Where you would take Sonny Rollins as a member of Miles Davis’ band, and then he would break away and start his own band. And she was saying that if musicians really sat down and thought about what they were doing, and kind of stuck together, and — but there are other things involved other than just the money part of it. You know, you really want to say what you want to say. And you probably can’t say everything that you want to say in Miles’ band. So you have to start your own band. So in a way she was right, and in a way she didn’t quite make too much sense.
Do you think that’s the scene happening today? Do you think musicians are pricing themselves out?
Sometimes I wonder, for instance, when you go to the Iridium for instance, and you end up spending sixty dollars, is the musician profiting from that? If so, great. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

You’re trying to help to keep the club open you know. The price of real estate in New York is so horrendous. It’s amazing that some of these clubs pay like twenty-five, thirty thousand a month rent or maybe more. Plus they have light bills on top of that and other things that go along with it. So everybody’s trying to just stay a little above the water you know. So I think everybody’s like I am. You just want to play man. You just want to play. I think that’s the only thing I’ve ever wanted to do in my life. Play jazz. And I still feel that way. I mean the thing that makes me happy is if I have a gig, with anybody, even with this band that we have, the thing to me that’s most important, being a leader, is for me to lay down some nice bass lines that everybody can play on, and if the band is happy and it flows into the audience, and the audience goes home happy, but you don’t bastardize yourself. You don’t give up your principles and stuff for that. You don’t do cockamamie things like, whatever, but just be true to yourself. And so that’s really what I’m about. Trying to be a good bass player. Trying to put a good foundation there.
